title: Structured Streaming, event time and recovery
summary: A stream is a table that keeps growing: micro-batches read it, a watermark decides when a window is final, the checkpoint remembers what was planned and committed, and only a keyed sink survives a replay without repeating itself.
outcomes: Trace one micro-batch from source offsets through state to the sink and name what the offset log, commit log and state store each hold.
Predict, batch by batch, the watermark, the windows a query emits in append mode and whether a late row counts.
Choose a trigger, a window and a watermark delay by weighing latency, completeness and state size, and tell event-time from processing-time results.
Explain where exactly-once holds and where it depends on the source, sink and operation, and design an idempotency key for a foreachBatch effect.
Restart a query from its checkpoint, predict what it replays, and recognise changes that the checkpoint cannot absorb.
startingAssumptions: The DataFrames and transformations module: typed columns, grouping and joins in SQL and PySpark.
The ingestion module's distinction between arrival order and the order records describe, and the Delta module's idea of a commit log.
editorialRationale: Streaming is taught through one real, bounded local run rather than a simulated loop: five files land in a fixed order, and every beat reads what Spark itself reported. The sequence starts with the table model and triggers, separates event time from processing time before introducing windows and the watermark, shows state and late rows batch by batch, then moves to output modes and joins, and only then to checkpoints, sink guarantees, a failure after downstream effects and the restart. Documented guarantees are kept apart from the one engine behaviour observed locally, which is labelled as observed.

claims.description: Structured Streaming treats a stream as an input table that keeps being appended; Spark runs the query incrementally, reading only new data, keeping only the intermediate state needed, and by default executing a series of small batch jobs called micro-batches.
claims.context: Apache Spark 4.0.4 programming model; Databricks runs the same engine with its own additions.

claims.description: With no trigger a micro-batch starts when the previous one ends; a fixed interval skips intervals without new data; the deprecated one-time trigger gives way to availableNow, which processes everything available at the start in one or more micro-batches, finishes uncommitted batches first, advances the watermark per batch, runs a final no-data batch when that moved the watermark, and stops; continuous processing is experimental and at-least-once.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 triggers; sources that cannot support availableNow fall back to a single batch.

claims.description: The file source processes new files in modification-time order, expects each file to appear atomically (for example by a move), limits new files per micro-batch with maxFilesPerTrigger, requires a user-specified schema by default, and is fault-tolerant.
claims.context: Open-source file source; Auto Loader is a separate Databricks source.

claims.description: Event time is the time embedded in the data rather than when Spark receives it; a window aggregation is a grouping on the event-time column in which each window is a group and one row can belong to several windows.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 programming model.

claims.description: Tumbling windows are fixed, non-overlapping and hold each input once; sliding windows are fixed but overlap when the slide is shorter than the window, so an input can fall in several; session windows grow while inputs keep arriving within a gap.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 window types.

claims.description: withWatermark(column, threshold) lets the engine keep a window's state, and let late data update it, until the maximum event time seen minus the threshold passes the window's end; in append mode the window's final result is written only then, after which its state is dropped.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4; the watermark lags the largest event time by the declared threshold.

claims.description: A watermark delay guarantees that data less late than the delay is never dropped; data later than the delay is not guaranteed to be dropped and may or may not be aggregated.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 semantic guarantee of aggregation with watermarking.

claims.description: Watermark-based state cleanup needs append or update output mode, an aggregation on the event-time column or on a window of it, and withWatermark on that same column before the aggregation; complete mode keeps all aggregation state.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 conditions for cleaning aggregation state.

claims.description: Append writes only result rows that will never change, which for an aggregation requires a watermark and delays each window by the threshold; update writes rows changed since the last trigger; complete rewrites the whole result table; an aggregation without a watermark cannot use append.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 output modes; joins support append only.

claims.description: The state store is a versioned key-value store that carries stateful operators across micro-batches; the default provider keeps state in executor JVM memory backed by checkpoint files, and the experimental state data source reads that state back from a checkpoint.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 state store; lab L08 read its state with the state data source.

claims.description: A stream-static join keeps no state; a stream-stream join buffers past rows of both inputs as state, which watermarks plus an event-time constraint bound; outer and semi joins must declare them, and outer NULL rows arrive only after the delay and time range have passed.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 join support matrix; queries with joins use append mode.

claims.description: With a checkpoint location a query records the offset range of each trigger in write-ahead logs and saves running aggregates, so after a failure or an intentional stop it continues where it left off.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 fault tolerance; the checkpoint belongs to one query.

claims.description: Restarting from the same checkpoint does not allow changing the number or type of input sources, nor any change to the schema of a stateful operation such as grouping keys or aggregates, because state is restored with the schema it was written with.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 recovery semantics after changes; other changes depend on the source, sink and query.

claims.description: End-to-end exactly-once needs a replayable source, the checkpointed engine and an idempotent sink; the file sink is exactly-once, the Kafka and foreach sinks are at-least-once, and foreachBatch depends on the function: at-least-once by default, exactly-once only if it uses the batch id or another key to deduplicate, with the semantics of any extra operations it applies left to the user.
claims.context: Spark 4.0.4 built-in sinks; platform sinks document their own guarantees.

claims.description: On Databricks a checkpoint records a query's offsets, commits and state; deleting or changing its location starts the query fresh, and each query needs its own checkpoint location.

claims.description: Databricks documents foreachBatch as receiving each micro-batch's output with its batch identity, leaves duplicate writes and failure handling to the sink logic, and requires stateful queries to consume each batch DataFrame completely.

concepts.definition: The streaming model's view of a source: a table that keeps receiving appended rows, queried incrementally.
concepts.example: After 02.json lands, Cinderline's input table has 10 rows, but batch 2 reads only the 4 new ones.

concepts.definition: One small batch job over the new input since the last one, with its own id, planned offsets and commit.
concepts.example: Batch 4 of the lab read 03.json's four rows under the 09:13:30 watermark.

concepts.definition: The setting that decides when a query starts its next micro-batch and whether it stops by itself.
concepts.example: trigger(availableNow=True) processed 01.json in two micro-batches and then stopped.

concepts.definition: A source's marker for how far a query has read, recorded per micro-batch in the offset log.
concepts.example: offsets/7 records file-source offset 3, meaning files up to 04.json.

concepts.definition: A query's own directory of offset log, commit log, source log and state, used to continue after a stop or failure.
concepts.example: After the failure the checkpoint held offsets 0-7 but commits 0-6.

concepts.definition: The versioned key-value store that keeps open windows and other stateful values between micro-batches.
concepts.example: After batch 5 the state held only 09:20 L1 (6 units) and 09:20 L3 (2 units).

concepts.definition: The time recorded in the event itself, when the thing happened at the source.
concepts.example: e011's event time is 09:03:00 even though its file landed at 09:28:00.

concepts.definition: The time the pipeline receives or processes a record, set by delivery rather than by the event.
concepts.example: Files 01 and 02 landed at 09:13 and 09:19, so a landing-time window puts 48 L1 units in 09:10-09:20.

concepts.definition: A time interval on the event-time column that acts as a grouping key: tumbling windows do not overlap, sliding windows do.
concepts.example: window(event_time, '10 minutes') places e007 at 09:09:30 in the 09:00-09:10 window.

concepts.definition: The largest event time seen minus a declared delay; windows ending at or before it are final.
concepts.example: After 03.json the watermark is 09:27:00 minus 5 minutes, 09:22:00.

concepts.definition: Rows that arrive after rows with later event times; too-late rows reach a window already finalized.
concepts.example: e011 (09:03:00) arrived after the 09:00 window was emitted and was counted as dropped.

concepts.definition: The rule for which result rows a trigger writes to the sink: new final rows, changed rows or all rows.
concepts.example: In append mode the 09:00 windows reached the sink once, after the watermark passed 09:10.

concepts.definition: A join between a streaming DataFrame and a static one; it keeps no streaming state.
concepts.example: Lab L08 joins each count event to the three-row line table to add the plant.

concepts.definition: A join between two streaming DataFrames that buffers both sides as state until watermarks allow cleanup.
concepts.example: Matching each press stop with a maintenance ticket within 30 minutes needs both streams buffered.

concepts.definition: The destination a streaming query writes each trigger's output to, with its own fault-tolerance guarantee.
concepts.example: The lab writes windows through foreachBatch and joined rows through the Parquet file sink.

concepts.definition: Each input affects the output once despite failures, needing a replayable source, the checkpoint and an idempotent sink.
concepts.example: The file sink kept 14 rows for 14 events across a stop and restart.

concepts.definition: A value that identifies one business effect, so a repeated attempt with the same key changes nothing.
concepts.example: The key 09:20|L1 stopped the replayed batch 7 from sending a second L1 message.

concepts.definition: Starting the same query definition on the same checkpoint so it resumes from the recorded offsets and state.
concepts.example: The restart replayed batch 7 only and read no committed file again.

concepts.definition: A window of dynamic length that stays open while inputs keep arriving within a gap duration.
concepts.example: A press producing counts every few minutes forms one session until it is idle for the gap.

concepts.definition: The rule that combines per-stream watermarks into the single watermark stateful operators use.
concepts.example: With min, a silent quality-hold stream holds back the watermark for the press stream too.

concepts.definition: Removing repeated events in a stream by identifier, keeping past identifiers as state until a watermark lets them go.
concepts.example: A gateway resending e016 twice is filtered by its event_id within the watermark delay.

concepts.definition: A state store provider that keeps state in native memory and local disk instead of the JVM heap.

visuals.title: The same late row, two outcomes
visuals.alt: The same late row, two outcomes. e011 is dropped when files arrive one run at a time and counted when they are processed as a backlog.
visuals.caption: Micro-batch boundaries, which are processing time, decided whether e011 counted; the documented guarantee allows both. Synthetic fixture, executed locally in lab L08.
visuals.textEquivalent:
One file per run: A no-data batch evicted the 09:00 window before 03.json arrived, so e011 had nowhere to go. Table columns: Batch, Previous watermark, This watermark, 09:00-09:10 L1. Rows: 3 (no data), 09:07:40, 09:13:30, emitted as 27 / 3, removed; 4 (03.json), 09:13:30, 09:13:30, gone: e011 dropped.

All files at once: No batch ran between 02.json and 03.json, so the window was still open when e011 arrived. Table columns: Batch, Previous watermark, This watermark, 09:00-09:10 L1. Rows: 1 (02.json), 1970-01-01 00:00:00, 09:07:40, open, 27 / 3; 2 (03.json), 09:07:40, 09:13:30, e011 counted, emitted as 36 / 4.

The rule both runs followed: Observed in local Spark 4.0.4 and confirmed in lab test 07: late rows are judged against the previous batch's watermark, eviction uses the current one. Equation: row counted if its window end > previous batch's watermark; window emitted once its end <= this batch's watermark.

visuals.alt: What the sink receives in each output mode. After the first two files, append sends only final windows, update sends changed windows, complete sends every window.

options.rationale: Committed input is never rescanned; the running totals come from the state store, not from rereading 01.json.

options.text: trigger(processingTime='1 hour')

options.text: 36, because the question is about when the parts were made, which is event time.
options.rationale: Correct: each count event carries the time it was made; landing time measures delivery, which lagged by up to 25 minutes here.

options.text: 48, because landing time is when Spark actually processed the rows.
options.rationale: Landing time answers when data reached the pipeline; it moves all four of L1's 09:00-09:10 events (e001, e003, e007, e011) into later windows.

options.text: 0, because no file had landed before 09:10.
options.rationale: True about arrival, but four L1 events were made in that window; they simply reached the pipeline later.

options.text: Either one, because both groupings total 126 units.
options.rationale: Equal totals over all windows do not make per-window answers interchangeable, and the question asks about one window.

options.rationale: Correct: with a 10-minute window and a 5-minute slide every event falls in exactly two windows, so each unit is counted twice.
That is the tumbling total; overlapping windows count an event once for every window it belongs to.
Sliding windows never split an event's units between windows; they repeat the whole event in each window.
That would need every event in three windows; a 10-minute window sliding every 5 minutes holds each event in two.

selfQuestions.prompt: After batch 5 the state holds 09:20 L1 (6 units) and 09:20 L3 (2 units); after batch 9 it holds only 09:40 L1 (8 units). Explain why each window is still in state at that point, what would remove it, and what that means for a dashboard that reads only emitted rows.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: A window stays in state until the watermark reaches its end. After batch 5 the watermark is 09:22:00, before the 09:20 windows end at 09:30, so they are open; an event later than 09:35:00 moves the watermark past 09:30 and the following batch emits and removes them. After batch 9 the watermark is 09:41:00 and the 09:40 window ends at 09:50, so it waits for an event later than 09:55:00. A dashboard fed from append mode shows neither window yet: the newest windows always lag by the window length plus the delay, and the last window before a quiet period can wait indefinitely.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Eviction is driven by the watermark, which moves only when later events arrive, so state size and dashboard lag are two views of the same rule. Answers that suggest update mode or a scheduled heartbeat event to show partial values sooner are acceptable.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline wants to (1) add each count event's plant from a small line table and (2) pair each press stop with the maintenance ticket raised within 30 minutes, keeping stops that never got a ticket. For each join, say what state Spark keeps, what must be declared, and when an unmatched stop appears in the output.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: (1) is a stream-static join: each micro-batch's new events join the whole static table and no streaming state is kept, which the lab executed with the three-row line table. (2) is a stream-stream left outer join: Spark buffers both stops and tickets as state. Both streams need a watermark, and the join needs an event-time range such as ticket_time between stop_time and stop_time plus 30 minutes; for an outer join these are required, not optional. An unmatched stop is written with NULL ticket columns only after the watermark shows no ticket can still arrive for it, roughly the 30-minute range plus the ticket stream's delay after the stop, and later if no new data advances the watermark.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Whether a join keeps state depends on whether the other side is static or streaming, and outer rows need proof that no match can still come. Noting that outer NULL rows may wait for new data to arrive is a correct refinement.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline's foreachBatch sends a 'window below target' alert for each finished window through an HTTP call. Design the idempotency key and where it is stored, and explain why checking the batch id alone would not have prevented the lab's duplicates if the id were recorded after sending.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Use the business identity of the alert: window start, line and alert type, for example 2026-09-14T09:20:00Z|L1|below-target. Store it in the receiving system, or in an outbox table written in the same transaction as the alert record, and have the sender skip, or the receiver reject, a key it already holds. A batch-id ledger written after the HTTP calls fails exactly like the lab: batch 7 sent three alerts, raised before recording anything, and the replay with the same batch id found no record and sent them again. The batch id is stable across replays, so it can be part of a key, but only if it is recorded atomically with the effect.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Idempotency needs a key that is identical on replay and a check that is atomic with the effect it guards. A keyed upsert into a table, such as a MERGE on window and line, is an acceptable alternative for data effects.

selfQuestions.prompt: The team wants to (a) add max(units) to the running windowed aggregation, (b) move the checkpoint to a tidier folder, and (c) raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 2 to 200. For each, predict what happens on restart and propose a safe way to make the change.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: (a) The aggregation's state schema changes, so restarting on the old checkpoint fails with STATE_STORE_VALUE_SCHEMA_NOT_COMPATIBLE, as the lab showed; deploy it as a new query with a new checkpoint, decide where it starts reading, and reconcile overlapping windows. (b) A new checkpoint location is a new query that starts from scratch: it would reread the landing directory and repeat downstream effects unless the sink is keyed, so move only with a planned start point. (c) The offset log records the shuffle partition count and a restart keeps it, as lab test 13 showed when the session asked for 3 and the query kept 2 state partitions; using a new count also needs a new checkpoint. Rehearse each change on a copy of the checkpoint first.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The checkpoint pins the source identity, the state schema and the state partitioning, so a change to any of them is a migration rather than a restart. Rehearsing on a copied checkpoint mirrors the lab's negative test.

beats.title: A stream is a table that keeps growing
beats.outcome: Describe a streaming query as an incremental query over an unbounded input table and say what each micro-batch reads.
beats.explanation: Structured Streaming treats arriving records as rows appended to an [[dbxfe-streaming-table-concept|unbounded input table]] and runs your query on it incrementally. Each [[dbxfe-streaming-microbatch-concept|micro-batch]] reads only the rows that arrived since the previous one and combines them with state carried forward. Notice in the second state that the table holds 10 rows, yet batch 2 read only the 4 rows of 02.json; the 09:00 totals of 27 and 23 came from state plus those rows, not from rereading 01.json.
beats.hint: Look at which file the second state marks as new, and where the earlier rows' contribution now lives.

handbook.markdown:
The programming model is the familiar SQL one: write the query as if the input were a table, and Spark runs it as an incremental query over a table that keeps receiving rows. Nothing materializes the whole input. Each trigger reads the new rows, updates the result using state kept from earlier batches, and lets the input rows go.

The lab's query is an ordinary grouped aggregation over a streaming DataFrame:

```python
events = (spark.readStream
          .schema("event_id STRING, line STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP, units INT")
          .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1)
          .json(landing_dir))
totals = (events.withWatermark("event_time", "5 minutes")
          .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "line")
          .agg(F.sum("units").alias("units"), F.count("*").alias("events")))
```

Three details come from the file source. It needs an explicit schema by default, so the schema cannot drift between a failure and a restart. It orders new files by modification time, and `maxFilesPerTrigger` caps how many new files one micro-batch takes. Files must appear whole, which is why the lab renames each file into the landing directory instead of writing it there.

What to inspect: each run's progress reports `numInputRows` per batch. In the recorded run the first batch after 02.json landed reported 4 rows, not 10, and the checkpoint's file-source log maps source offset 1 to 02.json alone. If a run ever reports the whole directory again, it is using a new checkpoint, which makes it a new query.

Not covered here: sources without replayable offsets, and Databricks Auto Loader, a different file source with its own options.

beats.recap: A streaming query is incremental: each micro-batch reads only new rows and carries everything else in state.

beats.title: The trigger decides when a micro-batch starts and whether the query stops
beats.outcome: Choose between the default, fixed-interval, availableNow and continuous triggers for a stated latency and cost need.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-trigger-concept|trigger]] sets the timing of micro-batches. Without one, the next batch starts as soon as the previous one ends; a fixed interval waits for the interval; availableNow processes everything present at the start, possibly in several batches, and then stops; the once trigger is deprecated; continuous processing is experimental. Notice in the second state that availableNow ran a second batch that read no rows: the watermark had moved, so it ran a no-data batch before stopping.
beats.hint: Which trigger both splits the backlog into several batches and terminates without being stopped?

handbook.markdown:
The trigger is a timing policy; the query logic does not change.

```python
writer = (df.writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_dir)
          .foreachBatch(write_windows))
# Choose one:
query = writer.trigger(processingTime="1 minute").start()  # a micro-batch each minute with new data
query = writer.trigger(availableNow=True).start()          # drain what is there, then stop
query = writer.start()                                     # next micro-batch as soon as the last ends
```

With no trigger a micro-batch starts as soon as the previous one completes. A fixed interval waits for the boundary; if a batch overruns it, the next one starts immediately, and no batch starts when no new data is available. The one-time trigger ran everything as a single micro-batch and is deprecated in favour of availableNow, which processes all data present when the run starts in as many micro-batches as the source options require, finishes uncommitted batches first, advances the watermark after each batch, runs one no-data batch at the end if the watermark moved, and terminates. Continuous processing is an experimental mode for millisecond latency with at-least-once guarantees and a restricted set of queries.

The choice is latency against cost. A scheduled availableNow run gives batch-like cost with streaming bookkeeping: checkpointed offsets, state and exactly-once processing. A continuously running query gives low latency but holds compute all day. In the lab every windowed run is availableNow, which is also what makes the lab bounded: each run stopped by itself once the files present had been processed, with no sleep and no manual stop.

What to inspect: batch ids and `numInputRows` in `recentProgress`. A no-data batch with 0 rows and a new watermark is expected under availableNow. A source that cannot support availableNow falls back to a single batch, losing the gradual watermark advance; check the source before relying on it.

beats.recap: Continuous service, fixed cadence, or availableNow to drain and stop: pick the trigger by latency and cost.

beats.title: Event time answers when it happened; processing time answers when it arrived
beats.outcome: Tell event-time from processing-time results and choose the clock a business question needs.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-streaming-eventtime-concept|Event time]] is a column in the record: when the press counted the parts. [[dbxfe-streaming-processingtime-concept|Processing time]] is when the pipeline received it. The lab grouped the same 18 events both ways. Notice in the third state that L1's units for 09:00-09:10 are 36 by event time but 0 by landing time, because no file had landed yet, while 09:10-09:20 reads 21 against 48. The totals agree at 126; only the per-window answers differ.

handbook.markdown:
Every record in a stream has at least two times. Event time is recorded by the source: the press stamped `event_time` when it counted the parts. Processing time is set by delivery: the gateway, the network and the landing directory decide when a record reaches Spark. The lab's batch comparison reads the same five files twice:

```python
events = (spark.read.schema(schema).json(landing_dir)
          .select("*", F.col("_metadata.file_modification_time").alias("landed_at")))
by_event = events.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "line").agg(F.sum("units"))
by_landing = events.groupBy(F.window("landed_at", "10 minutes"), "line").agg(F.sum("units"))
```

The file's modification time is its landing time, because the lab stamps each file before moving it in. Grouped by landing time, files 01 and 02 both fall into 09:10-09:20, so L1 shows 48 units there and nothing earlier; grouped by event time, L1 made 36 units in 09:00-09:10 and 21 in 09:10-09:20. The difference is pure delivery delay: L1's e001 and e003 landed at 09:13, e007 at 09:19 and e011 at 09:28, so none of L1's 09:00-09:10 units land in that window.

Use event time for questions about the business: output per shift, defects per hour, sales per day. Use processing time to measure the pipeline itself: throughput, arrival lag, how far behind the source you are. The price of event time is that a window can still receive rows after it ends, so the engine needs a rule for how long to wait; that rule is the watermark in the next beats.

What to inspect: the gap between a record's event time and its arrival. In this fixture e011 arrived 25 minutes after it happened; a delay chosen without measuring that gap is a guess. The same split applies to retail orders stamped at the till and uploaded in batches.

beats.recap: Report business activity by event time; use processing time to measure the pipeline itself.

beats.title: A window is a grouping key; sliding windows count each event more than once
beats.outcome: Predict which tumbling and sliding windows an event joins and what that does to totals.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-window-concept|window]] turns event time into a grouping key. Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, so each event lands in exactly one; sliding windows overlap when the slide is shorter than the window, so an event lands in several. Notice in the second state that e007 at 09:09:30 belongs to both 09:00-09:10 and 09:05-09:15, and in the third that the sliding rows sum to 252 units, twice the 126 the events carry.

handbook.markdown:
`window()` returns a struct with `start` and `end`, and grouping by it is ordinary grouping:

```python
tumbling = events.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "line").agg(F.sum("units"))
sliding = events.groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes", "5 minutes"), "line").agg(F.sum("units"))
```

Windows are half-open, `[start, end)`. e008 at exactly 09:05:00 belongs to the tumbling window 09:00-09:10 and to the sliding windows that start at 09:00 and at 09:05, but not to one that ends at 09:05. The lab's batch read produced 10 tumbling rows summing to 126 units and 21 sliding rows summing to 252.

Use tumbling windows for totals that must add up: units per 10 minutes, per shift, per day. Use sliding windows for a rolling view, such as the last 10 minutes refreshed every 5, and never sum their rows as a total. Session windows, built with `session_window`, have no fixed length: a session grows while events keep arriving within a gap and closes after a quiet period; they suit activity bursts rather than fixed reporting periods.

Windows also set the size of the state. Each open (window, line) pair is one state row; a sliding window with half the slide keeps roughly twice as many open rows. A window aggregation over a stream therefore costs memory in proportion to keys times open windows, which the watermark then bounds.

What to inspect: the `window.start` and `window.end` of output rows, and any total that is exactly a multiple of the expected figure, which usually means overlapping windows were summed.

beats.recap: Tumbling windows partition events; sliding windows overlap, so their rows are never summed as totals.

beats.title: The watermark trails the newest event time by a declared delay
beats.outcome: Compute the watermark after each arrival and say which windows it makes final.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-watermark-concept|watermark]] is the latest event time the query has seen minus the delay you declare with withWatermark. Spark recomputes it at the end of each micro-batch, and a window becomes final once the watermark reaches the window's end. Notice across the states: after 01.json the watermark is 09:07:40 and nothing is final; after 02.json it passes 09:10, so the 09:00 windows are emitted once; after 05.json the 09:40 window still waits.

samajh.text: Socho society ka doodhwala har subah parchi deta hai, jis par us din ki date likhi hoti hai. Parchiyan kabhi-kabhi der se pahunchti hain. Treasurer ka niyam hai: jo sabse nayi parchi dekhi hai, usse do din pehle tak ka hafta band. Jab tak hafta band nahi hua, der se aayi parchi bhi jud jaati hai. Band hafte ki parchi baad mein aaye, toh hisaab dobara nahi khulta.
samajh.mapping: Each slip's date is event time, the day it reaches the treasurer is processing time, a week is a window, the two-day allowance is the watermark delay, and closing a week is emitting its final result.
samajh.boundary: Spark recomputes the watermark once per micro-batch from the newest event time, and whether a too-late row still counts can depend on micro-batch boundaries, which a household account book does not have.

beats.hint: Subtract the delay from an event time, not from a landing time.

handbook.markdown:
The watermark turns "how long do we wait for late rows?" into a number the engine can act on:

```python
events.withWatermark("event_time", "5 minutes") \
      .groupBy(F.window("event_time", "10 minutes"), "line")
```

Declare it on the same column the window uses and before the aggregation; otherwise append mode refuses the query and state is never cleaned. At the end of each micro-batch Spark takes the largest event time seen so far and subtracts the delay. The next batch uses that value, and under availableNow a final no-data batch applies it before stopping.

| After | Largest event time | Watermark | Windows made final |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01.json | 09:12:40 | 09:07:40 | none |
| 02.json | 09:18:30 | 09:13:30 | 09:00 L1 27, L2 23 |
| 03.json | 09:27:00 | 09:22:00 | 09:10 L1 21, L2 18 |
| 04.json | 09:38:00 | 09:33:00 | 09:20 L1 6, L2 4, L3 2 |
| 05.json | 09:46:00 | 09:41:00 | 09:30 L2 3, L3 5 |

The delay is a trade. With 15 minutes instead of 5, the lab's transfer run counted every event, including e011, but each window was emitted one arrival later and 3 windows were still waiting at the end instead of 1. Choose it from the lateness you actually measure, the freshness the consumer needs and the state you can afford.

What to inspect: `eventTime.watermark` in each progress report, and `batchWatermarkMs` in the checkpoint's offset files. Limits: the watermark only moves when newer events arrive, so a quiet source holds its last windows open; with several input streams one global watermark applies, by default the slowest stream's.

beats.recap: Watermark = newest event time seen minus the delay; a window is final once the watermark reaches its end.

beats.title: State holds only the windows that can still change
beats.outcome: Read a state snapshot per batch and explain what enters, updates and leaves the state store.
beats.explanation: The [[dbxfe-streaming-state-concept|state store]] keeps one row per open window and line, versioned with each micro-batch and saved in the checkpoint. A batch's rows update those entries; the watermark removes the ones that are final. Notice in the lab's snapshots that four windows are open after batch 0, the 09:00 windows leave after batch 3, and after batch 9 only 09:40 L1 remains: with no later event, nothing can move the watermark past 09:50.

samajh.text: Mohalle ke darzi ki deewar par hook lage hain. Jin kapdon ki silai chal rahi hai, unki parchi hook par latakti hai, aur har nayi fitting par parchi badal di jaati hai. Kapda deliver hua, parchi hook se utar gayi. Deewar par sirf wahi kaam latakta hai jo abhi badal sakta hai, isliye deewar kabhi poori nahi bharti.
samajh.mapping: Each slip on a hook is one open window in the state store, a fitting is an update from a micro-batch, delivery is emitting the final window, and taking the slip down is state eviction.
samajh.boundary: The state store is versioned and checkpointed, so an earlier version can be rebuilt after a failure; the tailor's wall keeps no history and cannot replay yesterday's fittings.

handbook.markdown:
For the lab's aggregation a state row is keyed by `(window, line)` and holds the running `sum` and `count`. Each micro-batch loads the previous version, applies its rows, removes keys whose window end is at or before the watermark, and saves a new version under the checkpoint's `state/` directory, split by shuffle partition (two here: `state/0/0` and `state/0/1`).

Spark reports the effect of each batch in `stateOperators`: `numRowsTotal` after the batch, `numRowsUpdated`, `numRowsRemoved` and `numRowsDroppedByWatermark`. The lab also read the rows themselves with the experimental state data source, which in Spark 4.0 only reads:

```python
spark.read.format("statestore").option("batchId", 6).load(checkpoint_dir)
```

| After batch | Open windows (units / events) | Left the store in this batch |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 09:00 L1 22/2, L2 17/2; 09:10 L1 7/1, L2 11/1 | none |
| 3 | 09:10 L1 21/2, L2 15/2 | 09:00 L1, L2 (emitted) |
| 4 | 09:10 L1 21/2, L2 18/3; 09:20 L1 6/1, L3 2/1 | none; e011 dropped |
| 9 | 09:40 L1 8/1 | 09:30 L2, L3 (emitted) |

State size is keys times open windows. A longer delay, sliding windows, more lines or a stream-stream join all raise it; complete mode never removes anything. The default provider keeps state in executor JVM memory backed by checkpoint files; the RocksDB provider exists for very large state.

What fails: without a watermark an aggregation's state only grows, and a restart with a changed aggregation cannot load the state it wrote before. To show state honestly, read it back as the lab did rather than describing it.

beats.recap: State is the set of windows the watermark has not closed; it shrinks only when event time moves on.

beats.title: Late is judged per window, and too-late rows are not guaranteed to be dropped
beats.outcome: Predict whether a late row counts from its window end, the watermark and the micro-batch boundaries, and state the documented guarantee.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-streaming-late-concept|Late data]] is judged by its window's end, not by the row's own time: e008 at 09:05:00 was older than the 09:07:40 watermark yet counted, because its window ended at 09:10. e011 was dropped when a no-data batch had already evicted its window, but counted when the same files ran as a backlog. Notice in the third state the rule both runs followed. The documentation guarantees only that rows within the delay are kept.
beats.hint: Compare each row's window end with the watermark of the batch before the one that read it.

handbook.markdown:
Three rows from the lab show the whole rule.

- **e008**, made 09:05:00, read in batch 2 under the watermark 09:07:40. Older than the watermark, but its window ends at 09:10, after it, so the window was open and e008 counted: 09:00 L2 = 23.
- **e011**, made 09:03:00, in 03.json. Run one file at a time, batch 3 (a no-data batch, watermark 09:13:30) had already emitted and evicted 09:00 L1 as 27. Batch 4 reported `numRowsDroppedByWatermark = 1`, and 27 stayed 27.
- **e011 again**, with all files present before one run. No batch ran between 02.json and 03.json, so the window was still in state when e011 arrived; batch 2 counted it and emitted 36.

The lab confirmed the mechanism in local Spark 4.0.4: a stateful operator drops late rows by comparing their window end with the previous micro-batch's watermark, and evicts state with the current one. Switching the internal setting `spark.sql.streaming.statefulOperator.allowMultiple` to false made the backlog drop e011 too. That setting was used only to attribute the observation, never as a fix.

The documented contract is one-directional: a delay of 5 minutes guarantees that no row less than 5 minutes late is dropped; rows later than that may or may not be counted. So never build logic that depends on too-late rows disappearing, and never promise that they will be counted. If every row matters, choose the delay from measured lateness, and reconcile streaming results against a later batch recount over the same event-time windows.

What to inspect: `numRowsDroppedByWatermark` per batch. It counts drops but does not name them; to see which rows were dropped, compare the emitted windows with a batch aggregation, as the lab's event-time truth table does (36 against 27).

beats.recap: Rows within the delay always count; later rows may or may not, depending on when their window left state.

beats.title: Output mode decides which result rows the sink sees
beats.outcome: Choose append, update or complete for a query and predict what reaches the sink after each trigger.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-streaming-mode-concept|output mode]] decides which result rows each trigger writes. Append writes a row once, when it can no longer change, so an aggregation needs a watermark and waits for it. Update writes every row that changed in the trigger. Complete writes the whole result table and never drops state. Notice after 02.json: append sends the two final 09:00 windows, update sends four changed windows, and complete sends all four current windows.

handbook.markdown:
The mode is set on the writer and validated against the query when it starts:

```python
query = (totals.writeStream.outputMode("append")   # or "update", "complete"
         .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_dir)
         .foreachBatch(write_windows)
         .start())
```

| Query | Modes allowed | What that means |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregation with a watermark on event time | append, update, complete | append waits for the watermark; complete keeps all state |
| Aggregation without a watermark | update, complete | append is refused |
| Stream-stream join | append | update and complete are not supported yet |
| No aggregation | append, update | complete is not supported |

Choose by what the sink can do. Append suits sinks that cannot change a written row, such as the file sink, and consumers that want one final value per window, at the cost of waiting the window length plus the delay. Update suits a keyed store that upserts, for example a MERGE on window and line: it is fresher, but the same window arrives several times and the sink must overwrite, not add. Complete suits a small result table such as a live leaderboard, and its state never shrinks.

The lab executed append only; the update and complete rows in the visual are derived by hand from the documented rules. The negative test shows the start-time check: without the watermark, `start()` raised `STREAMING_OUTPUT_MODE.UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` before any batch was planned.

What to inspect: rows per trigger at the sink, and whether an update-mode consumer adds values it should replace; a doubled 09:00 total usually means that.

beats.recap: Append waits for final rows, update repeats changed rows, complete resends everything and keeps all state.

beats.title: A static side keeps no state; a second stream must be buffered
beats.outcome: Distinguish stream-static from stream-stream joins by the state they keep and the watermarks they need.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-static-join-concept|stream-static join]] matches each micro-batch's new rows against a static table and keeps nothing between batches; the lab added each event's plant this way. A [[dbxfe-streaming-stream-join-concept|stream-stream join]] must buffer both inputs, because a row can match one that has not arrived yet. Notice in the second state that watermarks on both sides plus a time-range condition decide when buffered rows are dropped, and outer NULL rows wait until then.

handbook.markdown:
The lab's stream-static join is one line, and it is stateless:

```python
enriched = events.join(lines, "line")   # lines = spark.createDataFrame(...) from fixtures/lines.json
```

It was stopped and restarted from its checkpoint, and the Parquet output held 14 rows for 14 events. A stream-stream join is different in kind. Any row from one side can match a future row from the other, so Spark keeps past rows of both sides in state. To bound that state you give each side a watermark and add an event-time constraint; the example below is a schematic and was not executed:

```python
stops = stops_stream.withWatermark("stop_time", "10 minutes")
tickets = tickets_stream.withWatermark("ticket_time", "20 minutes")
matched = stops.join(tickets, F.expr("""
    ticket_line = stop_line AND
    ticket_time >= stop_time AND
    ticket_time <= stop_time + interval 30 minutes"""), "leftOuter")
```

Documented support, in short: with the stream on the left and the static table on the right, inner, left outer and left semi joins are supported and stateless, while right and full outer joins are not. Stream-stream inner joins are supported, with watermarks and a time constraint optional but needed to clean state. Outer and semi joins must declare them. Outer NULL rows arrive only after the delay and the time range have passed, and may wait for new data, because watermarks advance when batches run. Queries with joins use append mode.

What to inspect: `numRowsTotal` of the join's state operator over time; steady growth means a missing watermark or time bound. With two streams one global watermark applies, by default the minimum, so a silent stream holds the join back.

beats.recap: Stream-static joins are stateless; stream-stream joins buffer both sides until watermarks and a time range release them.

beats.title: The checkpoint writes the plan before the batch and the commit after it
beats.outcome: Read a checkpoint's offset, commit, source and state entries and tell a committed batch from a planned one.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-checkpoint-concept|checkpoint]] is one query's own directory. Before a micro-batch runs, Spark writes its planned [[dbxfe-streaming-offset-concept|source offsets]] and watermark to offsets/N; after the sink returns, it writes commits/N with the next watermark. State versions and the file-source log sit beside them. Notice in the second state that offsets/7 exists but commits/7 does not: batch 7 was planned and its rows delivered, then the sink raised before the commit.

samajh.text: Bank mein passbook print karte waqt clerk pehle likhta hai: page 7 chhap raha hai, entries 31 se 36. Phir printer chalata hai, aur print poora hone par tick lagata hai. Agar beech mein printer atak gaya, toh agli baar woh wahi page 7, wahi entries, dobara chhaapta hai; page 1 se shuru nahi karta.
samajh.mapping: Writing down 'page 7, entries 31 to 36' first is the offset log entry, printing is running the micro-batch and its sink, the tick is the commit log entry, and reprinting page 7 is replaying the uncommitted batch.
samajh.boundary: A reprint only overwrites paper; a replayed micro-batch reruns code whose earlier external effects, such as messages already sent, are not undone by the checkpoint.

beats.hint: Which of the two logs is written before the batch runs?

handbook.markdown:
The lab reads the checkpoint of local Spark 4.0.4 directly, to see the mechanism. These files are an implementation detail for learning, not an interface to edit.

| Entry | Written | Holds (lab values) |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata` | once | the query id |
| `offsets/7` | before batch 7 runs | `v1`, then `batchWatermarkMs` (09:33:00), a map of settings such as `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` = 2, then `{"logOffset":3}` |
| `sources/0/3` | when offset 3 is planned | the file that offset covers: 04.json |
| `state/0/<partition>/` | while the batch runs | the new state version |
| `commits/7` | after the sink returns | `{"nextBatchWatermarkMs": ...}` for 09:33:00 |

The order is the point. The plan goes to the offset log first, so a restart can repeat the same batch with the same input range and the same watermark; the commit goes last, so a batch that failed anywhere, including inside your sink function, stays uncommitted. After the failure the lab found offsets 0-7 and commits 0-6, and

```python
sorted(set(logs["offsets"]) - set(logs["commits"]))   # -> [7]
```

names the batch the restart will finish first.

Rules that follow: one checkpoint belongs to one query and must not be shared; deleting it or pointing the query at a new location starts a new query from scratch, which re-reads the source and repeats downstream effects unless they are keyed; keep it on durable storage. When a stream will not start, read the checkpoint before changing anything: a gap between offsets and commits is normal after a failure and resolves itself on restart.

beats.recap: offsets/N is the plan written first, commits/N is written last; a gap between them is the batch a restart will replay.

beats.title: Exactly-once depends on the source, the engine and the sink together
beats.outcome: Say where end-to-end exactly-once holds for a pipeline and name the sinks that give only at-least-once.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-streaming-exactly-once-concept|Exactly-once]] output needs three parts: a source that can replay by offset, the checkpointed engine, and a [[dbxfe-streaming-sink-concept|sink]] that tolerates a repeated batch. The built-in file sink records committed files in its own log, so the lab's join kept 14 rows for 14 events across a stop and a restart. Notice the warnings in the first state: Kafka and foreach sinks are at-least-once, and foreachBatch is only as strong as the function you write.

handbook.markdown:
Spark's guarantee is stated as a chain. Sources have offsets and can be replayed from them; the engine records each batch's offset range and state in the checkpoint; sinks are idempotent for reprocessing. Break one link and the guarantee becomes at-least-once.

| Sink | Documented guarantee | Why |
|---|---|---|
| File (Parquet, JSON, ...) | exactly-once | its `_spark_metadata` log names the files each committed batch wrote |
| Kafka | at-least-once | a replay can publish the same records again |
| foreach | at-least-once | your per-row code runs again on replay |
| foreachBatch | depends on the implementation | at-least-once by default; deduplicate with the batch id or a key |
| console, memory | debugging only | not fault-tolerant |

The source matters as much. The file source is replayable because the files stay in place; a message source needs retention longer than your longest outage. Platform sinks such as Delta Lake tables document their own guarantees; check the current documentation for the runtime you use rather than assuming.

The lab shows both ends. The stream-static join wrote through the file sink, was stopped with `stop()`, restarted from its checkpoint, and ended with 14 rows and 14 distinct event ids; the sink's own log listed batches 0, 1 and 2. The windowed query wrote through foreachBatch, failed once after its effects, and its naive outbox held 10 messages for 7 windows right after the replay and 12 for 9 at the end of the run.

The operation matters too. Inside foreachBatch you may run operations the engine cannot plan incrementally, or write one batch to several places, but then the end-to-end semantics of those operations are yours to reason about, and each extra write can recompute the batch unless it is persisted first. On Databricks, foreachBatch receives each micro-batch with its batch id, and a stateful query must consume the whole batch DataFrame, as the lab does with one `collect()` of a tiny result. Exactly-once is not always needed: an alert that is safe to repeat, or a consumer that deduplicates, can accept at-least-once, provided someone decided that deliberately.

beats.recap: Processing is exactly-once through the checkpoint; output is exactly-once only when the sink is idempotent or transactional.

beats.title: A replayed batch repeats every effect it already made
beats.outcome: Design an idempotency key for a foreachBatch effect and show why a naive effect duplicates after a replay.
beats.explanation: After a failure, the restart replays the uncommitted batch with the same id and the same rows, which is correct engine behaviour. Anything the first attempt already did outside Spark happens again. Notice the two states: the naive outbox appends the three 09:20 messages a second time and ends with 12 messages for 9 windows, while the keyed outbox finds each window|line [[dbxfe-streaming-idempotency-concept|idempotency key]] already sent and ends with 9.

samajh.text: Society ke gate par guard ke paas parcel ki list hai, har parcel ke AWB number ke saath. Courier wala galti se wahi parcel dobara le aaye, toh guard number milaata hai aur kehta hai: yeh toh aa chuka. Jis gate par aisi list nahi, wahan residents ko ek hi cheez do baar mil jaati hai.
samajh.mapping: The AWB number is the idempotency key, the guard's list is the keyed outbox's record of sent keys, the second delivery is the replayed micro-batch, and the gate without a list is the naive outbox.
samajh.boundary: The list protects only if the number is written down in the same step as accepting the parcel; a guard who notes numbers later can still let a duplicate through if interrupted in between.

handbook.markdown:
The lab arms its sink to raise after it has delivered the 09:20 windows. The engine then did exactly what it promises: batch 7 stayed uncommitted, and the restart called the function again with batch id 7 and the same three rows. The failure sits between the effect and the commit, which is where real failures happen: a timeout after the HTTP call succeeded, a worker lost after writing.

```python
def send_windows(batch_df, batch_id):
    for row in batch_df.collect():                       # tiny output; one action consumes the batch
        key = f"{row.window.start:%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ}|{row.line}"
        if outbox.insert_if_absent(key, render(row)):    # illustrative helper: check and record atomically
            deliver(key)                                 # illustrative helper: the external effect
```

Choose the key from the business fact, not from the attempt. A window and a line identify one finished result; the batch id identifies one micro-batch and is also stable across replays, so either can be part of the key. What decides correctness is atomicity: the key must be recorded in the same step as the effect, or checked by the receiver. A ledger written after sending misses exactly this failure. For data rather than messages, a MERGE on the key into a table is the same idea.

Demonstrate it honestly the way the lab does: inject a failure after the effect, restart, and count. Naive outbox 7 then 10 then 12; keyed outbox 7 then 7 then 9; the keyed table of window results was identical before and after the replay.

Limits: `collect()` is only for small outputs; larger ones should be written as a DataFrame with a keyed MERGE. The lab's outboxes are Python lists, not a real messaging system.

beats.recap: Key every external effect by its business identity and record that key in the same step as the effect.

beats.title: Restart the same query on the same checkpoint, or plan a migration
beats.outcome: Predict what a restart replays and decide when a change needs a new checkpoint and a planned start point.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-streaming-restart-concept|restart]] starts the same query definition on the same checkpoint. It finishes uncommitted batches first, then plans only new data. Notice the table: after the failure, the first restart replays batch 7 and writes commits/7; the second plans nothing; 05.json is then read alone. The last state shows the limit: an aggregation with one more column cannot reuse the state and fails with STATE_STORE_VALUE_SCHEMA_NOT_COMPATIBLE.

handbook.markdown:
A restart is only a restart when three things are unchanged: the query's sources, its stateful operators and its checkpoint location. Then it resumes. In the lab the first restart after the failure replayed batch 7 alone; the next restart found nothing to plan (Spark still posted one progress report, numbered 8, with zero input rows, but wrote no offset file and never called the sink); and after 05.json landed, batch 8 read that file's 2 rows and nothing else.

Changes the documentation rules out between restarts: a different number or type of input sources, and any change to the schema of a stateful operation, such as grouping keys or aggregates, deduplication columns, or a stream-stream join's type or keys. The lab's negative test added `max(units)` and failed with `STATE_STORE_VALUE_SCHEMA_NOT_COMPATIBLE`, leaving offsets 0-2 and commits 0-1. Some settings are pinned too: test 13 set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to 3 before restarting, yet every offset entry still recorded 2 and the state kept two partitions.

For a change that the checkpoint cannot absorb, plan a migration:

1. Deploy the new query with a new checkpoint location.
2. Decide its start point: which files or offsets it may read, and which windows it owns.
3. Make downstream effects keyed, so any overlap cannot double-send.
4. Reconcile overlapping windows against a batch recount before switching consumers.

Operating it: a scheduler or job with retries restarts a failed query on the same checkpoint, which is exactly the replay path above. Watch `recentProgress` for the replayed batch id. Never delete a checkpoint to make an error go away; that starts a new query from the beginning of the source.

beats.recap: Same query and same checkpoint means resume; a changed stateful query means a new checkpoint and a planned start point.

extensionCards.prompt: When would a session window group Cinderline's press events better than a 10-minute tumbling window?
extensionCards.answer: When the question is about bursts of activity, such as one production run: a session stays open while events keep arriving within the gap and closes after a quiet period.
extensionCards.explanation: session_window gives windows of dynamic length: a session starts with an event, extends while further events arrive within the gap duration, and closes when none arrives for the gap. A press run that starts at 09:02 and pauses at 09:47 becomes one session rather than five tumbling windows, which answers how long and how productive each run was instead of how much was made per 10 minutes. Sessions still need a watermark to be finalized and to release state, and their length is not known in advance. They were not executed in lab L08, so check the behaviour on your runtime before relying on it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It shows that the window shape follows the business question, and that dynamic windows still depend on the watermark.

extensionCards.prompt: Cinderline unions its press stream with a quality-hold stream that goes silent for an hour. What happens to the watermark by default?
extensionCards.answer: It stops advancing, because the global watermark is the minimum of the streams' watermarks, so windows wait for the silent stream instead of dropping its rows.
extensionCards.explanation: Spark tracks each input stream's maximum event time and combines the resulting watermarks into one global watermark for stateful operators. The default policy takes the minimum, so no stream's rows are dropped as too late only because another stream is ahead; the cost is that results wait for the slowest stream. Setting spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy to max lets the watermark follow the fastest stream and emits sooner, but drops the slower stream's data more aggressively. Choose it only when the business accepts losing the lagging stream's late rows. Lab L08 reads a single stream, so this was not executed.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It explains a common symptom of stuck output in multi-stream jobs and the documented trade-off of changing it.

extensionCards.prompt: Cinderline's gateway sometimes resends a file's events. How can the stream drop repeated event_ids without keeping every id forever?
extensionCards.answer: Deduplicate on event_id with a watermark: include the event-time column in the deduplication, or use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark, so old identifiers leave state.
extensionCards.explanation: Streaming deduplication keeps the identifiers it has seen as state. Without a watermark it must keep every identifier forever. With withWatermark on event_time and deduplication on both event_id and event_time, old identifiers are removed once the watermark passes them. If a resent event can carry a different timestamp, dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark deduplicates on event_id alone within the watermark delay, which should be longer than the largest gap between duplicates. This removes duplicate input; it does not make a foreachBatch effect idempotent, which still needs its own key. Not executed in lab L08.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It separates duplicate input from replayed output and shows how a watermark bounds the state that deduplication needs.

extensionCards.prompt: Why would a query tracking millions of machine keys switch to the RocksDB state store provider?
extensionCards.answer: Because the default provider keeps state in executor JVM memory, where millions of objects cause long garbage-collection pauses; RocksDB keeps state in native memory and on local disk.
extensionCards.explanation: The default HDFS-backed provider holds state objects in the executors' JVM heap and writes changes to the checkpoint. With millions of keys, garbage-collection pauses make micro-batch durations swing. Since Spark 3.2 the RocksDB provider keeps state in native memory and on local disk, and still saves changes to the checkpoint for the same fault tolerance. It is chosen with spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass; the lab's offset files record that setting next to the shuffle partitions, a sign that it belongs to the query's checkpoint, so plan a provider change as a migration. Managed runtimes can use different defaults; check before sizing memory.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It connects state size to memory behaviour and treats the state store provider as a design decision tied to the checkpoint.

recap.title: A growing table, a moving watermark and a checkpoint that remembers
recap.markdown: **A stream is a table that keeps growing, processed one micro-batch at a time.** Event time says when something happened; the watermark, newest event time minus a declared delay, says when a window is final, and only open windows stay in state. Rows within the delay always count; later rows may or may not, depending on when their window left state. The checkpoint writes each batch's plan before it runs and its commit after the sink returns, so a restart replays exactly the uncommitted batch. That makes processing exactly-once, not your sink's side effects: key every external effect by its business identity. **Transfer challenge:** a parcel carrier streams scan events from vans that upload only when back in range. Choose the event-time column, a window and a delay, say which scans a 20-minute delay could lose, and design the key for a 'parcel delivered' notification that must never be sent twice.

appliedTask.title: Predict a sixth file, then fail it on purpose
appliedTask.prompt: The lab's one-file-per-run sequence (scenario S in the lesson) has processed 05.json: the watermark is 09:41:00 and the state holds only 09:40 L1 (8 units, 1 event). 06.json now lands at 09:59 with e019 (L3, 09:39:30, 4 units), e020 (L1, 09:58:00, 6 units) and e021 (L2, 09:44:00, 5 units). Predict batch by batch the input rows, the watermark used, the rows dropped, the state after each batch and what the sink receives. Then say what the naive and keyed outboxes hold if the sink fails after sending in the batch that emits the 09:40 windows, and propose one change if the plant needs e019 counted.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Batch 10 reads 3 rows under the watermark 09:41:00. e019 belongs to 09:30-09:40, which batch 9 emitted and removed, so it is dropped (numRowsDroppedByWatermark = 1). e021 opens 09:40 L2 and e020 opens 09:50 L1: 2 keys updated, 3 state rows (09:40 L1 8/1, 09:40 L2 5/1, 09:50 L1 6/1), nothing sent. Batch 11 is a no-data batch with watermark 09:58:00 minus 5 minutes, 09:53:00, past 09:50: it emits 09:40 L1 8/1 and 09:40 L2 5/1 and leaves only 09:50 L1 in state. If the sink fails after sending, batch 11 stays uncommitted and the restart replays it with the same two rows: the naive outbox goes from 12 to 14 and then 16, the keyed outbox from 9 to 11 and stays there. To count e019, the delay must keep 09:30-09:40 open when e019 arrives: the previous batch's watermark must still be before 09:40, so with the latest event at 09:46 the delay must exceed 6 minutes; the 15-minute delay of the transfer run would count it, at the cost of later results. Alternatively keep 5 minutes for fast alerts and reconcile daily totals with a batch recount by event time. The batch predictions were checked once on local Spark 4.0.4 by adding this file to the lab's sequential run.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer applies the three rules the lab asserted to a changed dataset: late rows are judged by window end against the previous batch's watermark, state is evicted at the current watermark, and a restart replays the uncommitted batch. It keeps engine behaviour separate from sink behaviour and treats the delay as a trade-off rather than a fix.
